group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old man who lives with his spouse in a single-story suburban house was brought to the emergency department by paramedics late this morning after two days of rigors, a progressively wetter cough, and shortness of breath that escalated while he was eating breakfast. According to his wife, he awoke drenched in sweat at 04:00, measured an oral temperature of “about 104 on the old Fahrenheit thermometer,” declined acetaminophen so that an unaltered fever could be documented, and soon began to breathe so rapidly that conversation became punctuated by panting. Emergency medical services arrived within fifteen minutes; they recorded numbers but deliberately withheld oxygen, intravenous fluids, and antipyretics in order to preserve baseline physiology, then transported him on ambient air during the nine-minute ride. Past illnesses include a long-standing ischemic cardiomyopathy diagnosed after an anterior wall infarction twelve years ago, for which he takes carvedilol, low-dose furosemide, and a morning dose of lisinopril; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months prior showed an ejection fraction of 30 – 35 % with a concentric remodeling pattern but no significant valvular lesion. He is also followed by nephrology for stage 4 chronic kidney disease attributed to diabetic-hypertensive injury; baseline creatinine hovers near 2.8 mg/dL and urea nitrogen has been in the high 40s for several years. He performs all activities of daily living independently, drives himself to appointments, and mows a small lawn with frequent breaks, denying any prior strokes, transient ischemic attacks, seizures, or memory lapses. He has never been admitted to a skilled nursing facility, does not carry a malignancy diagnosis, and has no history of chronic liver pathology. Medications taken at 06:00 — before symptom escalation — included his usual metformin, low-dose aspirin, and long-acting insulin glargine; he skipped the morning loop diuretic because of poor appetite. He quit smoking three decades ago after 20 pack-years, enjoys one glass of scotch on holidays, and denies illicit drug use. He received both pneumococcal vaccines over the past decade and an inactivated influenza shot seven weeks earlier. On arrival the patient sat upright on the stretcher, clutching a disposable emesis bag that he had been using to collect thick yellow sputum; speech was coherent, he stated the correct date, and answered all questions appropriately without delay. Skin was hot and flushed, mucous membranes appeared tacky, and jugular venous contour measured approximately 5 cm above the sternal angle, unchanged from cardiology documentation. Pre-intervention vital signs recorded by the trauma bay nurse were: rectal temperature 40.0 °C, pulse 82 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm confirmed by three-lead telemetry, non-invasive blood pressure 101 / 58 mm Hg verified manually, respirations counted for a full minute at 54 breaths min⁻¹ with pronounced intercostal retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry 96 % while still on room air at sea-level altitude. Capillary refill time was under two seconds; there was mild bilateral pedal edema consistent with his chronic baseline. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft S3 in addition to normal S1 and S2, no murmurs or rubs. Lung examination demonstrated bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles throughout the right middle and lower posterior fields with scattered rales over the left base; percussion remained largely resonant, and no meniscus or stony dullness was detected. The abdomen was soft with normal bowel sounds and a non-palpable liver edge. A focused neurologic screen showed equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in proximal and distal muscle groups. A bedside glucometer, obtained before venipuncture, read 190 mg/dL. Venous and arterial samples were drawn through separate sticks within ten minutes of roll-in, preceding any saline flush larger than that required to keep the heparin lock patent. Initial chemistry returned sodium 167 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 109 mEq/L, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 62 mg/dL, and creatinine 3.0 mg/dL; glucose by serum chemistry confirmed the finger-stick value at 190 mg/dL. A complete blood count revealed leukocytes 17.8 × 10⁹/L with 89 % neutrophils, hematocrit 47 %, hemoglobin 15.6 g/dL, and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. The arterial blood gas obtained on room air showed pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, PaO₂ 100 mm Hg, calculated bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, and base deficit −9, indicating a primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory alkalotic compensation. Serum lactate measured 3.1 mmol/L. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph taken before antibiotics or fluids demonstrated a dense consolidation occupying the right lower lobe with air bronchograms, clear costophrenic angles, and a cardiac silhouette of chronic borderline prominence; no layering fluid was identified. Electrocardiography displayed sinus rhythm at 80 beats min⁻¹ with old anterior Q waves and nonspecific ST-T flattening unchanged from an outpatient tracing. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a multiplex respiratory viral panel were dispatched prior to any empirical therapy. At the instant this note is dictated, he has received no intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, antipyretics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, diuretics, or supplemental oxygen, so every physiologic observation and laboratory datum above represents his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, and test-result points from the untreated presentation.
- Demographics: a man's age in years is his base score, so age 74 gives 74 points. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy +10; chronic renal disease +10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease: +0.
- Examination: respiratory rate 54/min (≥30) +20; temperature 40.0°C (<35 or ≥40) +15. Normal mentation, systolic pressure 101 mm Hg (not <90), and pulse 82/min (not ≥125): +0.
- Tests: arterial pH 7.20 (<7.35) +30; BUN 62 mg/dL (≥30) +20. Sodium is not <130 mEq/L, glucose is not ≥250 mg/dL, hematocrit is not <30%, PaO₂ is not <60 mm Hg, and there is no pleural effusion: +0.
Total = 74 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 15 + 30 + 20 = 179 (risk class V).
Final answer: 179
